Use Pydantic Settings: declare your values as attributes on a `BaseSettings` subclass, and they'll be read from environment variables when you create the settings object.

**1. Install the package.** Add the `pydantic-settings` package to your project[4] with `uv add pydantic-settings`.

**2. Create a `Settings` class.** Import `BaseSettings` from Pydantic and create a sub-class, very much like with a Pydantic model.[4] The same way as with Pydantic models, you declare class attributes with type annotations, and possibly default values.[4]

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    secret_key: str


settings = Settings()
app = FastAPI()
```

When you create an instance of that `Settings` class (in this case, in the `settings` object), Pydantic will read the environment variables in a case-insensitive way[4]. For example, `DATABASE_URL` will be read for `database_url`. Next it will convert and validate the data.[4]

**3. Pass the values when running the server.**

```console
$ DATABASE_URL="..." SECRET_KEY="..." uv run fastapi run main.py
```

In Bash, to set multiple env vars for a single command, separate them with a space and put them all before the command.[1] In Windows PowerShell, set each one first with `$Env:NAME = "value"`, then run the server.

**Optional: use a `.env` file.** If you have many settings that possibly change a lot, maybe in different environments, it might be useful to put them on a file and then read them from it as if they were environment variables.[5] For this to work, add `python-dotenv` to your project with `uv add python-dotenv`.[5] You can read more at Pydantic Settings: Dotenv (.env) support.[5]

The full guide is at https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/advanced/settings/
